claim: The study skeletonised 853 muscle cells in volume electron microscopy data covering an entire larva of the annelid Platynereis.
source: To study desmosomal networks, we skeletonised 853 muscle cells and their desmosomal partners in volume electron microscopy data covering an entire larva of the annelid Platynereis.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of muscle cells reconstructed and the organism studied.

claim: Muscle cells in the Platynereis larva adhere to other muscle cells, epithelial cells, glial cells, ciliated cells, bristle-producing cells, and the basal lamina.
source: Muscle cells adhere to each other, to epithelial, glial, ciliated, and bristle-producing cells and to the basal lamina, forming a desmosomal connectome of over 2000 cells.
evidence: The abstract directly lists the cell types to which muscle cells adhere.

claim: The desmosomal connectome comprises over 2000 cells.
source: Muscle cells adhere to each other, to epithelial, glial, ciliated, and bristle-producing cells and to the basal lamina, forming a desmosomal connectome of over 2000 cells.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the total number of cells in the desmosomal connectome.

claim: Aciculae are chitin rods that form an endoskeleton in the segmental appendages.
source: The aciculae – chitin rods that form an endoskeleton in the segmental appendages – are highly connected hubs in this network.
evidence: The abstract provides a definition of aciculae.

claim: Aciculae are highly connected hubs in the desmosomal network.
source: The aciculae – chitin rods that form an endoskeleton in the segmental appendages – are highly connected hubs in this network.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the connectivity status of aciculae in the network.

claim: The high connectivity of aciculae agrees with the many degrees of freedom of their movement.
source: This agrees with the many degrees of freedom of their movement, as revealed by video microscopy.
evidence: The abstract states that video microscopy revealed many degrees of freedom in acicular movement, which is consistent with their high connectivity.

claim: Mapping motoneuron synapses to the desmosomal connectome allowed inference of the extent of tissue influenced by motoneurons.
source: Mapping motoneuron synapses to the desmosomal connectome allowed us to infer the extent of tissue influenced by motoneurons.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that combining synaptic and desmosomal data enabled inference about motoneuron influence.

claim: Cellular-level maps of synaptic and adherent force networks can elucidate body mechanics.
source: Our work shows how cellular-level maps of synaptic and adherent force networks can elucidate body mechanics.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement about the utility of the approach.

claim: Animals use somatic muscles to rapidly change body shape.
source: Animals use somatic muscles to rapidly change body shape.
evidence: The introduction states this as a general principle of animal physiology.

claim: Whole-body shape changes can drive swimming, crawling, or other forms of movement.
source: Whole-body shape changes can drive swimming, crawling, or other forms of movement.
evidence: The introduction describes the functional outcomes of body shape changes.

claim: Moving appendages with exo- or endoskeletons and joints can have many degrees of freedom to support walking, flying, and several other functions.
source: Moving appendages with exo- or endoskeletons and joints can have many degrees of freedom to support walking, flying, and several other functions.
evidence: The introduction describes the functional capabilities of appendages with skeletal support.

claim: A large diversity of muscles with differential nervous control is required for appendage movement (Brierley et al., 2012; Charles et al., 2016; Cruce, 1974; Landmesser, 1978; McKellar et al., 2020).
source: This requires a large diversity of muscles with differential nervous control (Brierley et al., 2012; Charles et al., 2016; Cruce, 1974; Landmesser, 1978; McKellar et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies supporting the need for muscle diversity.

claim: Contracting muscles must attach to other body parts to exert force and induce movements.
source: To exert force and induce movements, contracting muscles must attach to other body parts.
evidence: The introduction states this as a fundamental principle of muscle function.

claim: In many animals, muscle–force coupling is provided by desmosomes.
source: In many animals, muscle–force coupling is provided by desmosomes – stable adhesive junctions anchored by intracellular intermediate filaments.
evidence: The introduction describes the role of desmosomes in force transmission.

claim: Desmosomes are stable adhesive junctions anchored by intracellular intermediate filaments.
source: In many animals, muscle–force coupling is provided by desmosomes – stable adhesive junctions anchored by intracellular intermediate filaments.
evidence: The introduction provides a structural definition of desmosomes.

claim: Desmosomes occur in cardiac and somatic muscles of both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Desmosomes occur in cardiac and somatic muscles of both vertebrates and invertebrates.
evidence: The introduction states the taxonomic distribution of desmosomes.

claim: In the zebrafish heart, desmosomes connect cardiac myocytes to each other (Lafontant et al., 2013).
source: In the zebrafish heart for example, desmosomes connect cardiac myocytes to each other (Lafontant et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction cites a specific example of desmosomal connections in zebrafish.

claim: In the lamprey, desmosomes frequently unite adjacent muscle fibres for lateral force transmission (Nakao, 1975).
source: In the lamprey, desmosomes frequently unite adjacent muscle fibres for lateral force transmission (Nakao, 1975).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on desmosomal function in lamprey.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, hemidesmosomes link the pharyngeal muscles to the basement membrane (Albertson and Thomson, 1976).
source: In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, hemidesmosomes link the pharyngeal muscles to the basement membrane (Albertson and Thomson, 1976)
evidence: The introduction cites a study on hemidesmosomes in C. elegans pharyngeal muscles.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, body-wall muscles connect to hypodermal cells that lie underneath the cuticle via hemidesmosomes (Francis and Waterston, 1991).
source: and the body-wall muscles to hypodermal cells that lie underneath the cuticle (Francis and Waterston, 1991).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on body-wall muscle connections in C. elegans.

claim: In leech, muscle cells have a high density of hemidesmosomes anchoring the cells to the basal lamina (Pumplin and Muller, 1983).
source: In leech, muscle cells have a high density of hemidesmosomes anchoring the cells to the basal lamina (Pumplin and Muller, 1983).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on hemidesmosomes in leech muscle cells.

claim: In polychaete annelids, hemidesmosomes and desmosomes are common on the extracellular matrix connecting muscles and epithelial cells (Purschke, 1985).
source: In polychaete annelids, hemidesmosomes and desmosomes are common on the extracellular matrix connecting muscles and epithelial cells (Purschke, 1985).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on desmosomes in polychaete annelids.

claim: In Echiura, hemidesmosomes connect the chaetal follicle cells to the extracellular matrix (Tilic et al., 2015).
source: In Echiura, hemidesmosomes connect the chaetal follicle cells to the extracellular matrix.
evidence: The introduction cites a study on hemidesmosomes in Echiura.

claim: In Echiura, muscle cells have dense plaques linking them to the extracellular matrix opposite the sites where chaetal follicle cells connect (Tilic et al., 2015).
source: Opposite these sites, muscle cells have dense plaques also linking them to the extracellular matrix (Tilic et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction cites a study describing muscle cell connections in Echiura.

claim: Desmosomal connections form a body-wide network through which tensile forces propagate.
source: These desmosomal connections form a body-wide network through which tensile forces propagate.
evidence: The introduction describes the functional role of the desmosomal network.

claim: The desmosomal network comprises all muscles and all their cellular and non-cellular partners.
source: This network comprises all muscles and all their cellular and non-cellular (e.g. basal lamina) partners.
evidence: The introduction defines the components of the desmosomal network.

claim: The desmosomal connectome has muscles, other cells and basal lamina chunks as nodes and hemidesmosomes and desmosomes as links.
source: We refer to this network as the desmosomal connectome, with muscles, other cells and basal lamina chunks as nodes and hemidesmosomes and desmosomes as links.
evidence: The introduction defines the terminology and structure of the desmosomal connectome.

claim: How desmosomal networks are organised on the scale of the whole body in animals with complex muscles and appendages is not known.
source: How such networks are organised on the scale of the whole body in animals with complex muscles and appendages is not known.
evidence: The introduction identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Whole-body neuronal connectomes exist (Cook et al., 2019; Ryan et al., 2016; Verasztó et al., 2020; White et al., 1986).
source: While whole-body neuronal connectomes (where links are synaptic connections) exist (Cook et al., 2019; Ryan et al., 2016; Verasztó et al., 2020; White et al., 1986)
evidence: The introduction cites multiple studies that have produced whole-body neuronal connectomes.

claim: No whole-body desmosomal connectome has yet been described.
source: to our knowledge, no whole-body desmosomal connectome (where links are desmosomes) has yet been described.
evidence: The introduction states that this is the first whole-body desmosomal connectome.

claim: Desmosomal connections are not directional and do not represent signal flow.
source: Unlike synapses, desmosomal connections are not directional and do not represent signal flow.
evidence: The introduction contrasts desmosomal connections with synaptic connections.

claim: Desmosomal connections indicate physical coupling where the movement of one cell will result in the movement of the connected structure.
source: Rather they indicate physical coupling where the movement of one cell will result in the movement of the connected structure.
evidence: The introduction describes the functional meaning of desmosomal connections.

claim: The desmosomal connectome of larval Platynereis dumerilii was reconstructed from serial electron microscopy images of an entire larva (Randel et al., 2015).
source: To study the organisation of a body-wide tensile network and its motor control, here we reconstruct the desmosomal connectome of larval Platynereis dumerilii from serial electron microscopy images (volume EM) of an entire larva (Randel et al., 2015).
evidence: The introduction states the source of the EM data used for reconstruction.

claim: Platynereis dumerilii is a marine annelid worm that is increasingly used as a laboratory animal (Özpolat et al., 2021).
source: P. dumerilii or 'the nereid' is a marine annelid worm that is increasingly used as a laboratory animal (Özpolat et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction cites a review describing the use of Platynereis as a model organism.

claim: In Platynereis, muscle development starts in the planktonic, ciliated trochophore larval stage (1–2 days old) (Fischer et al., 2010).
source: In Platynereis, muscle development starts in the planktonic, ciliated trochophore larval stage (1–2 days old) (Fischer et al., 2010).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on muscle development in Platynereis.

claim: Older (around 3–6 days) nectochaete larvae have three main trunk segments, each with a pair of appendages called parapodia.
source: The older (around 3–6 days) nectochaete larvae have three main trunk segments, each with a pair of appendages called parapodia.
evidence: The introduction describes the anatomy of nectochaete larvae.

claim: The parapodia are composed of a ventral lobe (neuropodium) and a dorsal lobe (notopodium) and each lobe contains a single acicula and a bundle of chitin bristles (chaetae) (Hausen, 2005).
source: The parapodia are composed of a ventral lobe (neuropodium) and a dorsal lobe (notopodium) and each lobe contains a single acicula and a bundle of chitin bristles (chaetae) (Hausen, 2005).
evidence: The introduction cites a study describing parapodial anatomy.

claim: Platynereis larvae have an additional cryptic segment between the head and the main trunk segments (Steinmetz et al., 2011).
source: Platynereis larvae have an additional cryptic segment between the head and the main trunk segments (Steinmetz et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites a study identifying the cryptic segment.

claim: The cryptic segment (segment 0) lacks parapodia and gives rise to the anterior pair of tentacular cirri that start to grow around 3 days of development.
source: This cryptic segment – also referred to as segment 0 – lacks parapodia and gives rise to the anterior pair of tentacular cirri that start to grow around 3 days of development.
evidence: The introduction describes the characteristics of segment 0.

claim: Nectochaete larvae can either swim with cilia (Jékely et al., 2008) or crawl on the substrate by muscles (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Lauri et al., 2014).
source: Nectochaete larvae can either swim with cilia (Jékely et al., 2008) or crawl on the substrate by muscles (Conzelmann et al., 2013; Lauri et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites studies on larval locomotion modes.

claim: Trunk muscles support turning in swimming larvae during visual phototaxis (Randel et al., 2014).
source: Trunk muscles also support turning in swimming larvae during visual phototaxis (Randel et al., 2014)
evidence: The introduction cites a study on the role of trunk muscles in phototaxis.

claim: Trunk muscles mediate a startle response characterised by whole-body contraction and the elevation of the parapodia (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).
source: and mediate a startle response characterised by whole-body contraction and the elevation of the parapodia (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a study on the startle response.

claim: Older (>6-day-old) feeding juvenile stages are mainly crawling and develop a muscular, eversible proboscis (Fischer et al., 2010).
source: Older (>6-day-old) feeding juvenile stages are mainly crawling and develop a muscular, eversible proboscis (Fischer et al., 2010)
evidence: The introduction cites a study on juvenile development.

claim: Older (>6-day-old) feeding juvenile stages develop a moving gut with visceral muscles (Brunet et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2015).
source: a moving gut with visceral muscles (Brunet et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2015)
evidence: The introduction cites studies on gut development.

claim: Older (>6-day-old) feeding juvenile stages develop several sensory appendages (palps, antennae, and cirri).
source: and several sensory appendages (palps, antennae, and cirri).
evidence: The introduction describes the development of sensory appendages.

claim: Platynereis larvae (1- to 6-day-old stage) are 150–300 µm long and thus amenable to whole-body volume-EM analysis.
source: Platynereis larvae (1- to 6-day-old stage) are 150–300 µm long and thus amenable to whole-body volume-EM analysis.
evidence: The introduction states the size of larvae and its suitability for EM analysis.

claim: The study used a previously reported whole-body serial TEM dataset of a 3-day-old P. dumerilii larva (Randel et al., 2015).
source: To analyse the organisation of the somatic musculature, we used a previously reported whole-body serial TEM dataset of a 3-day-old P. dumerilii larva (Randel et al., 2015).
evidence: The Results section states the source of the EM data.

claim: All differentiated muscle cells were reconstructed by tracing along their longitudinal axis (skeletonisation) and marking the position of their soma.
source: First, we reconstructed all differentiated muscle cells by tracing along their longitudinal axis (skeletonisation) and marking the position of their soma (Figure 1, Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section describes the reconstruction method and references figures showing the results.

claim: All other cells in the larva, including neuronal and non-neuronal cells, were also skeletonised (Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: We also skeletonised all other cells in the larva, including neuronal and non-neuronal cells (see below and Verasztó et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section states that all cells were reconstructed and cites a previous study.

claim: 853 mononucleated muscle cells were identified in the whole-body volume.
source: We identified 853 mononucleated muscle cells in the whole-body volume.
evidence: The Results section explicitly states the total number of muscle cells identified.

claim: Most muscle cells have an obliquely striated ultrastructure, with the exception of developing muscle cells and the two MUSmed_head cells which have disorganised myosin filaments.
source: Most of them have an obliquely striated ultrastructure, with the exception of developing muscle cells (which contain few myosin filaments), and the two MUSmed_head cells which have disorganised myosin filaments.
evidence: The Results section describes the ultrastructural characteristics of muscle cells.

claim: The majority of muscle cells in the 3-day-old larva are somatic muscles.
source: The majority of muscle cells in the 3-day-old larva are somatic muscles (Table 1).
evidence: The Results section states the predominant muscle type and references a table.

claim: Most visceral muscles, including gut muscles, develop at a later stage (Brunet et al., 2016).
source: Most visceral muscles, including gut muscles, develop at a later stage (Brunet et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites a study on the timing of visceral muscle development.

claim: All muscle cells were classified into eight main groups: longitudinal, anterior and posterior oblique, chaetal, acicular, transverse, digestive system (developing), and head muscles.
source: Based on their position and shape, we classified all muscle cells into eight main groups (Figure 2, Table 1): longitudinal, anterior and posterior oblique, chaetal, acicular, transverse, digestive system (developing), and head muscles.
evidence: The Results section describes the classification scheme and references figures and tables.

claim: The eight main muscle groups could be further subdivided into 53 distinct types.
source: The eight main muscle groups could be further subdivided into 53 distinct types (Figure 2, Table 1, Video 1).
evidence: The Results section states the total number of muscle types identified.

claim: The 53 muscle types represent anatomically distinct groups of cells classified based on their position, shape, motoneuron inputs, and desmosomal partners.
source: These 53 types represent anatomically distinct groups of cells that we classified based on their position, shape, motoneuron inputs, and desmosomal partners.
evidence: The Results section describes the criteria used for cell type classification.

claim: All types are composed of segmentally repeated sets with the same number of cells on the left and right body sides, with few exceptions.
source: All types are composed of segmentally repeated sets with the same number of cells on the left and right body sides, with few exceptions (Figure 2I; Table 1).
evidence: The Results section describes the stereotypy of muscle cell types.

claim: The precise and repeated features of the anatomy and the type-specific patterns of desmosomal connectivity and motoneuron innervation suggest that these 53 types represent cell types specified by unique development programmes and muscle identity genes, as is the case for example in Drosophila larvae (de Joussineau et al., 2012).
source: The precise and repeated features of the anatomy and the type-specific patterns of desmosomal connectivity and motoneuron innervation suggest that these 53 types represent cell types specified by unique development programmes and muscle identity genes, as is the case for example in Drosophila larvae (de Joussineau et al., 2012).
evidence: The Results section infers developmental mechanisms based on anatomical observations and cites a comparative example.

claim: The majority of muscle types (34 out of 53 types corresponding to 502 out of 853 cells) are in the parapodial appendages and form the parapodial muscle complex.
source: The majority of muscle types (34 out of 53 types corresponding to 502 out of 853 cells) are in the parapodial appendages and form the parapodial muscle complex (Video 2).
evidence: The Results section quantifies the proportion of muscle types in the parapodial complex.

claim: The parapodial complex of the first segment in the 3-day-old larva has the same major muscle groups as other segments, but fewer muscle cells and some minor subgroups are missing (MUSac-neuDy, MUSac-neuDx, and MUSobP-M).
source: The parapodial complex of the first segment in the 3-day-old larva has the same major muscle groups as other segments, but fewer muscle cells and some minor subgroups are missing (MUSac-neuDy, MUSac-neuDx, and MUSobP-M).
evidence: The Results section describes segmental variation in muscle composition.

claim: The parapodia of the first segment will transform into tentacular cirri during cephalic metamorphosis (Fischer et al., 2010), but at the 3-day-old stage these are bona fide locomotor appendages.
source: The parapodia of this segment will transform into tentacular cirri during cephalic metamorphosis (Fischer et al., 2010), but at the 3-day-old stage these are bona fide locomotor appendages.
evidence: The Results section cites a study on developmental fate and describes the current functional state.

claim: The 3-day-old larva has a cryptic segment (segment 0) which lacks parapodia and has few muscle cells.
source: The 3-day-old larva also has a cryptic segment (segment 0) (Steinmetz et al., 2011), which lacks parapodia and has few muscle cells (Figure 2I, Table 1).
evidence: The Results section describes the characteristics of segment 0 and cites a previous study.

claim: Desmosomes can be identified as dark electron-dense plaques on cell membranes with a lighter electron-dense extracellular core area (desmoglea).
source: Desmosomes can be identified as dark electron-dense plaques on cell membranes with a lighter electron-dense extracellular core area (desmoglea).
evidence: The Results section provides morphological criteria for identifying desmosomes in EM images.

claim: Intracellular intermediate filaments frequently connect to the electron-dense desmosome plaques.
source: Intracellular intermediate filaments frequently connect to the electron-dense desmosome plaques.
evidence: The Results section describes the ultrastructural features of desmosomes.

claim: Desmosomes are enriched at the ends of muscle cells indicating that they transmit force upon muscle cell contraction.
source: Desmosomes can span multiple 40 nm EM layers (up to 15 layers) and are enriched at the ends of muscle cells indicating that they transmit force upon muscle cell contraction (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section infers functional significance from the spatial distribution of desmosomes.

claim: The (hemi-)desmosomal partners of muscle cells include the basal lamina (34.4% of desmosomes) and a diversity of cell types.
source: The (hemi-)desmosomal partners of muscle cells include the basal lamina (34.4% of desmosomes) and a diversity of cell types.
evidence: The Results section quantifies the proportion of desmosomes connecting to the basal lamina.

claim: Desmosomal partners of muscle cells include other muscle cells, glia, multiciliated cells of the ciliary bands (except the prototroch), epidermal cells, and various follicle cells encircling the chaetae and the aciculae.
source: These are other muscle cells, glia, multiciliated cells of the ciliary bands (except the prototroch), epidermal cells, and various follicle cells encircling the chaetae (chaetal follicle cells) and the aciculae (acicular follicle cells)(Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section lists the cell types that form desmosomal connections with muscles.

claim: Only 2.4% of (hemi-)desmosomes are between muscle cells and 60.5% of these are between different muscle types.
source: Only 2.4% of (hemi-)desmosomes are between muscle cells and 60.5% of these are between different muscle types.
evidence: The Results section quantifies the proportion of muscle-to-muscle desmosomes.

claim: In the Platynereis larva, desmosomes do not mediate lateral force transmission between muscles of the same bundle.
source: This suggests that in the Platynereis larva, desmosomes do not mediate lateral force transmission between muscles of the same bundle.
evidence: The Results section infers functional significance from the low proportion of muscle-to-muscle desmosomes.

claim: In many desmosomal partner cell types – but not in the muscle cells themselves – tonofibrils could be identified.
source: In many desmosomal partner cell types – but not in the muscle cells themselves – we could identify tonofibrils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section describes the distribution of tonofibrils across cell types.

claim: The full desmosomal connectome is an undirected graph of 2807 interconnected nodes (2095 with a soma) connected by 6961 edges.
source: The full desmosomal connectome is an undirected graph of 2807 interconnected nodes (2095 with a soma) connected by 6961 edges.
evidence: The Results section quantifies the size of the desmosomal connectome graph.

claim: Six hundred and thirty nodes are fragments of the basal lamina of similar skeleton sizes.
source: Six hundred and thirty nodes are fragments of the basal lamina of similar skeleton sizes (see Methods).
evidence: The Results section describes the composition of the connectome nodes.

claim: The Leiden algorithm detected several dense clusters of nodes or communities in the desmosomal connectome that correspond to anatomical territories in the larval body.
source: To characterise the structure of the desmosomal network, we first analysed its modularity by the Leiden algorithm, which partitions graphs into well-connected communities (Traag et al., 2019). We detected several dense clusters of nodes or communities in the desmosomal connectome. These communities correspond to anatomical territories in the larval body (Figure 3, Video 3).
evidence: The Results section describes the modularity analysis and its anatomical interpretation.

claim: There are four modules consisting of left and right ventrolateral and left and right dorsolateral longitudinal muscles spanning all body segments, and associated ciliary band and epidermal cells.
source: There are four modules – a left and right ventrolateral and a left and right dorsolateral – consisting of longitudinal muscles spanning all body segments, and associated ciliary band and epidermal cells.
evidence: The Results section describes specific modules identified in the analysis.

claim: Various head and segment-0 muscles constitute another module.
source: Various head and segment-0 muscles constitute another module (Figure 3, Video 3).
evidence: The Results section describes another module identified in the analysis.

claim: Two modules contain left–right groups of parapodial and oblique muscles in the second and third segments, connected at the midline through the basal lamina and the median ventral longitudinal muscle (axochord or MUSax) (Lauri et al., 2014; Purschke and Müller, 2006).
source: Two modules contain left–right groups of parapodial and oblique muscles in the second and third segments, connected at the midline through the basal lamina and the median ventral longitudinal muscle (axochord or MUSax) (Lauri et al., 2014; Purschke and Müller, 2006).
evidence: The Results section describes modules and cites studies on the axochord.

claim: The other modules include parapodial muscles and chaetal sac cells, in the segmental parapodia.
source: The other modules include parapodial muscles and chaetal sac cells, in the segmental parapodia.
evidence: The Results section describes the composition of additional modules.

claim: Each module contains muscles and epidermal cells, and various other cell types.
source: Each module contains muscles and epidermal cells, and various other cell types (Figure 3C).
evidence: The Results section describes the cellular composition of modules.

claim: The desmosomal graph stands out as a highly modular and less compact graph with strong local connectivity compared to simulated networks and the synaptic connectome.
source: While all graph types have a similar degree and weighted degree distribution (Figure 4A, B), the desmosomal graph stands out as a highly modular and less compact graph with strong local connectivity. This conclusion is supported by several graph measures.
evidence: The Results section compares the desmosomal graph to other graph types using multiple metrics.

claim: The modularity scores of the subsampled desmosomal graphs are higher than for any other graph types, including the synaptic connectome.
source: The modularity scores of the subsampled desmosomal graphs are higher than for any other graph types, including the synaptic connectome (Figure 4C).
evidence: The Results section presents a specific graph metric comparison.

claim: The desmosomal subgraphs have the largest graph diameter and the mean of the distances between vertices, both measures of graph compactness (Doyle and Graver, 1977).
source: The desmosomal subgraphs have the largest graph diameter (the length of the longest graph geodesic between any two vertices) and the mean of the distances between vertices (Figure 4D, E), both measures of graph compactness (Doyle and Graver, 1977).
evidence: The Results section presents graph metrics and cites a reference for their interpretation.

claim: The desmosomal and synaptic connectome graphs have the highest transitivity values (clustering coefficient), which measures the probability that nodes connected to the same node are also directly connected to each other.
source: The desmosomal and synaptic connectome graphs have the highest transitivity values (clustering coefficient), which measures the probability that nodes connected to the same node are also directly connected to each other (Figure 4F).
evidence: The Results section presents another graph metric comparison.

claim: The number of 3-cliques (three fully connected nodes) ranks the synaptic graph as first followed by the desmosomal graph.
source: A similar measure, the number of 3-cliques (three fully connected nodes) also ranks the synaptic graph as first followed by the desmosomal graph (Figure 4G).
evidence: The Results section presents another graph metric comparison.

claim: The assortativity coefficient is lowest for the desmosomal graph, indicating more connections between nodes of different degree.
source: The assortativity coefficient (between −1 and 1), a measure of the extent to which nodes of similar degree are connected (1 for the preferential-attachment graphs) is lowest for the desmosomal graph, indicating more connections between nodes of different degree (Figure 4H).
evidence: The Results section presents and interprets the assortativity coefficient.

claim: The desmosomal graph is characterized by high modularity, large diameter, large average distance, and high level of local connectivity (cliques).
source: Overall, the desmosomal graph stands out as a highly modular graph with a large diameter, large average distance, and high level of local connectivity (cliques).
evidence: The Results section summarizes the key characteristics of the desmosomal graph.

claim: These properties set the desmosomal graph apart from different types of random graphs and the synaptic connectome.
source: These properties set the desmosomal graph apart from different types of random graphs and the synaptic connectome.
evidence: The Results section contrasts the desmosomal graph with other graph types.

claim: The special organization of the desmosomal connectome is attributed to all cells only connecting to cells in their immediate neighbourhood forming local cliques, and without long-range connections.
source: We attribute these characteristics to the special organisation of the desmosomal connectome, with all cells only connecting to cells in their immediate neighbourhood forming local cliques, and without long-range connections (e.g. between the left and right body sides).
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation for the observed graph properties.

claim: In the force-field layout, nodes are segregated by body side and body segment.
source: To analyse how closely the force-field-based layout of the desmosomal connectome reflects anatomy, we coloured the nodes in the graph based on body regions (Figure 5). In the force-field layout, nodes are segregated by body side and body segment.
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial organization of nodes in the force-field layout.

claim: The observation that node positions in the force-field layout of the graph recapitulate the anatomical positions of the nodes reflects the local connectedness (neighbours only) of the desmosomal connectome.
source: The observation that node positions in the force-field layout of the graph recapitulate the anatomical positions of the nodes reflects the local connectedness (neighbours only) of the desmosomal connectome.
evidence: The Results section interprets the correspondence between graph layout and anatomy.

claim: This is different from the synaptic connectome where long-range neurite projections can link neurons at two different ends of the body (Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: This is different from the synaptic connectome where long-range neurite projections can link neurons at two different ends of the body (Verasztó et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section contrasts the desmosomal connectome with the synaptic connectome and cites a previous study.

claim: In the segmented larva, each parapodium has a dorsal and a ventral lobe (notopodium and neuropodium).
source: In the segmented larva, each parapodium has a dorsal and a ventral lobe (notopodium and neuropodium).
evidence: The Results section describes the anatomy of the parapodium.

claim: Each lobe is supported by an internal chitinous rod called acicula that is ensheathed by acicular follicle cells.
source: Each lobe is supported by an internal chitinous rod called acicula (Hausen, 2005) that is ensheathed by acicular follicle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, C).
evidence: The Results section describes the structure of the acicula and cites a previous study.

claim: Each parapodial lobe contains a chaetal sac consisting of bristle-producing chaetoblasts, chaetal follicle cells, epidermal cells, and bristle mechanosensory neurons (chaeMech) (Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: Each parapodial lobe also contains a chaetal sac consisting of bristle-producing chaetoblasts, chaetal follicle cells, epidermal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C), and bristle mechanosensory neurons (chaeMech) (Verasztó et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section describes the composition of the chaetal sac and cites a previous study.

claim: The chaetal follicle cells ensheathing the chaetae have four types arranged in a proximo-distal pattern.
source: The chaetal follicle cells ensheathing the chaetae have four types arranged in a proximo-distal pattern (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section describes the organization of chaetal follicle cells.

claim: The aciculoblasts, chaetoblasts, and the various follicle cells serve as anchor points for several major parapodial muscle groups.
source: The aciculoblasts, chaetoblasts, and the various follicle cells serve as anchor points for several major parapodial muscle groups (Figure 6E–I, Figure 1E, Video 4).
evidence: The Results section describes the functional role of follicle cells in muscle attachment.

claim: The aciculae and associated structures in the parapodial complex represent highly connected components in the desmosomal connectome.
source: The aciculae and associated structures in the parapodial complex represent highly connected components in the desmosomal connectome (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The Results section describes the connectivity of aciculae in the network.

claim: The cells with the largest mean degree and weighted degree belong to the parapodial complex.
source: The cells with the largest mean degree and weighted degree belong to the parapodial complex.
evidence: The Results section identifies the most highly connected cells in the network.

claim: 16 muscle types have connections to the aciculae or to acicular follicle cells.
source: We identified 16 muscle types with connections to the aciculae or to acicular follicle cells (Figure 6F, G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The Results section quantifies the number of muscle types connected to aciculae.

claim: These include acicular muscles (MUSac), some chaetal muscles (MUSchae) that link the aciculae to the chaetae and oblique muscles (MUSob) that link the aciculae to the dorsal longitudinal muscles (MUSlongD).
source: These include acicular muscles (MUSac), some chaetal muscles (MUSchae) that link the aciculae to the chaetae and oblique muscles (MUSob) that link the aciculae to the dorsal longitudinal muscles (MUSlongD).
evidence: The Results section describes the types of muscles connected to aciculae.

claim: Several acicular muscles attach on one end to the proximal base of the aciculae and on the other end to the paratrochs and epidermal cells.
source: Several acicular muscles attach on one end to the proximal base of the aciculae and on the other end to the paratrochs and epidermal cells.
evidence: The Results section describes the attachment sites of acicular muscles.

claim: Oblique muscles attach to the basal lamina, epidermal, and midline cells at their proximal end, run along the anterior edge of parapodia and attach to epidermal and chaetal follicle cells at their distal tips.
source: Oblique muscles attach to the basal lamina, epidermal, and midline cells at their proximal end, run along the anterior edge of parapodia and attach to epidermal and chaetal follicle cells at their distal tips (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Videos 2 and 4).
evidence: The Results section describes the attachment sites and trajectory of oblique muscles.

claim: Both acicular and oblique muscle groups are involved in moving the entire parapodium.
source: Both of these muscle groups are involved in moving the entire parapodium.
evidence: The Results section infers the functional role of these muscle groups.

claim: Acicular muscles move the proximal tips of the aciculae, while oblique muscles move the parapodium by moving the tissue around the chaetae and the aciculae.
source: Acicular muscles move the proximal tips of the aciculae, while oblique muscles move the parapodium by moving the tissue around the chaetae and the aciculae.
evidence: The Results section describes the distinct mechanisms by which different muscle groups move the parapodium.

claim: All acicular movements also correspond to parapodial movements.
source: All acicular movements also correspond to parapodial movements.
evidence: The Results section states the relationship between acicular and parapodial movements.

claim: Chaetae are embedded in the parapodium and therefore move with it, but the chaetal sac muscles can also independently retract the chaetae into the parapodium or protract them and make them fan out.
source: Chaetae are embedded in the parapodium and therefore move with it, but the chaetal sac muscles can also independently retract the chaetae into the parapodium or protract them and make them fan out.
evidence: The Results section describes the movements of chaetae and their relationship to parapodial movements.

claim: The notopodial and neuropodical aciculae have distinct muscle partners indicating that these structures could move independent of each other.
source: The notopodial and neuropodical aciculae have distinct muscle partners indicating that these structures could move independent of each other.
evidence: The Results section infers functional independence from distinct connectivity patterns.

claim: Two muscles (MUSac-i and MUSac-neuDx) link the noto- and neuropodial aciculae within the same parapodium to each other, suggesting force coupling between the two aciculae.
source: Two muscles (MUSac-i and MUSac-neuDx) link the noto- and neuropodial aciculae within the same parapodium to each other, suggesting force coupling between the two aciculae (Figure 6E, G).
evidence: The Results section identifies muscles that couple the two aciculae and infers their functional role.

claim: Analysis of each muscle group for their desmosomal partners and spatial orientation revealed several possible acicular movements termed extension, flexion, pivoting, abduction, chaetal retraction, and jostling.
source: We analysed each muscle group for their desmosomal partners and spatial orientation and inferred the possible movements of the aciculae upon their contraction. This revealed several possible acicular movements which we termed extension, flexion, pivoting, abduction, chaetal retraction, and jostling (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, Video 2, Video 4).
evidence: The Results section describes the inference of acicular movements from anatomical data.

claim: Some muscles connect to epidermal cells in the parapodium and through moving these epidermal cells can indirectly also move the aciculae (i.e. 'pulled by the skin'; e.g. MUSobP-neuV).
source: In addition, some muscles connect to epidermal cells in the parapodium and through moving these epidermal cells can indirectly also move the aciculae (i.e. 'pulled by the skin'; e.g. MUSobP-neuV) (Video 4).
evidence: The Results section describes an indirect mechanism of acicular movement.

claim: The movement of the parapodia during crawling requires connections to the axochord muscle (MUSax) at the midline.
source: The movement of the parapodia during crawling also requires connections to the axochord muscle (MUSax) at the midline.
evidence: The Results section describes the role of the axochord in parapodial movement.

claim: Animals with an ablated axochord show impaired crawling indicating a structural role for this muscle (Lauri et al., 2014).
source: Animals with an ablated axochord show impared crawling indicating a structural role for this muscle (Lauri et al., 2014).
evidence: The Results section cites an experimental study demonstrating the functional importance of the axochord.

claim: A high density of hemidesmosomes between the axochord and the extracellular matrix dorsal to the neuronal midline agrees with a structural role for the axochord.
source: A high density of hemidesmosomes between the axochord and the extracellular matrix dorsal to the neuronal midline agrees with this (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D).
evidence: The Results section relates anatomical observations to functional inferences.

claim: The extracellular matrix on the midline serves as an attachment site for the proximal ends of anterior and posterior oblique muscles and the radial-glia-like midline cells that are rich in tonofibrils.
source: The extracellular matrix on the midline also serves as an attachment site for the proximal ends of anterior and posterior oblique muscles and the radial-glia-like midline cells that are rich in tonofibrils.
evidence: The Results section describes the attachment sites on the midline extracellular matrix.

claim: The desmosomal connectome suggests that each acicula can have complex and extensive movements and the two aciculae can move independently of each other, with some coupling.
source: The desmosomal connectome suggests that each acicula can have complex and extensive movements and the two aciculae can move independently of each other, with some coupling (e.g. through the inter-acicular muscles).
evidence: The Results section summarizes inferences about acicular movements from the connectome data.

claim: The organization of the musculature in 3- and 4-day-old three-segmented larvae is very similar.
source: The organisation of the musculature in 3- and 4-day-old three-segmented larvae is very similar (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), therefore we could relate movements in the more active 4-day-old larvae to the EM data.
evidence: The Results section justifies the use of 4-day-old larvae for movement analysis by comparing their musculature to 3-day-old larvae.

claim: DeepLabCut was used to train a deep residual neural network to track and label 26 body parts of the larvae.
source: We used the toolbox DeepLabCut (Mathis et al., 2018) to train a deep residual neural network using sample video frames to learn, track, and label 26 body parts of the larvae.
evidence: The Results section describes the method used for tracking body parts.

claim: The notopodial and neuropodial aciculae within one parapodium exhibit differences in movement velocity and angles relative to one another resulting in a range of angles and positions over time.
source: We found that the notopodial and neuropodial aciculae within one parapodium exhibit differences in movement velocity and angles relative to one another resulting in a range of angles and positions over time (Figure 7, Video 5).
evidence: The Results section describes the observed movements of aciculae from video tracking.

claim: During the crawl cycles, the aciculae first draw inwards and forwards, diagonally towards the head, then they tilt in a posterior direction, the proximal tip of the neuropodial acicula travelling slightly faster to open up the pair, creating the larger (40–50°) inter-acicular angle.
source: During the crawl cycles, the aciculae first draw inwards and forwards, diagonally towards the head, then they tilt in a posterior direction, the proximal tip of the neuropodial acicula travelling slightly faster to open up the pair, creating the larger (40–50°) inter-acicular angle (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: The Results section describes the sequence of acicular movements during crawling.

claim: The acicular cycle is completed by a 'piston' movement whereby the now parallel aciculae are pushed outwards, then the proximal tips tilt rostrally again, to move the chaetae back against the trunk, propelling the animal forward on that side.
source: This is followed by a 'piston' movement whereby the now parallel aciculae are pushed outwards, then the proximal tips tilt rostrally again, to move the chaetae back against the trunk, propelling the animal forward on that side and completing that acicular cycle.
evidence: The Results section describes the completion of the acicular movement cycle.

claim: The acicular pairs can have different relative positions with inter-acicular angles changing between −25° and 50° in one parapodial cycle.
source: This analysis demonstrates that the acicular pairs can have different relative positions with inter-acicular angles changing between −25° and 50° in one parapodial cycle (Figure 7B, G).
evidence: The Results section quantifies the range of inter-acicular angles during movement.

claim: These relative changes occur in each segment during crawling, propagating from posterior to anterior through an undulatory gait cycle.
source: These relative changes occur in each segment during crawling, propagating from posterior to anterior through an undulatory gait cycle (Figure 7A).
evidence: The Results section describes the spatial and temporal pattern of acicular movements during crawling.

claim: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial acicular muscle (MUSac-neuPV) pulls the proximal end of the acicula caudally, inducing an abduction.
source: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial acicular muscle (MUSac-neuPV) pulls the proximal end of the acicula caudally, inducing an abduction (Figure 7H; Figure 6—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: The Results section describes the movement induced by a specific muscle contraction observed in live imaging.

claim: MUSac-neuPV muscles connect to the proximal end of the acicula via acicular follicle cells and anchor to the basal lamina, epidermal cells and ciliated cells (paratroch) at their other end.
source: These muscles connect to the proximal end of the acicula via acicular follicle cells and anchor to the basal lamina, epidermal cells and ciliated cells (paratroch) at their other end (Figure 7K).
evidence: The Results section describes the desmosomal connectivity of MUSac-neuPV.

claim: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial muscles (MUSobP-neuV) induces an inward movement of the distal tip of the acicula ('flexion') leading to the alignment of the parapodia and chaetae with the longitudinal body axis.
source: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial muscles (MUSobP-neuV) induces an inward movement of the distal tip of the acicula ('flexion', Figure 6—figure supplement 4B) leading to the alignment of the parapodia and chaetae with the longitudinal body axis (Figure 7I).
evidence: The Results section describes the movement induced by MUSobP-neuV contraction.

claim: MUSobP-neuV cells connect to the distal end of the aciculae via acicular follicle cells and also connect to epidermal cells in the neuropodium. At their other end, MUSobP-neuV cells are anchored to the basal lamina.
source: These muscles connect to the distal end of the aciculae via acicular follicle cells and also connect to epidermal cells in the neuropodium. At their other end, MUSobP-neuV cells are anchored to the basal lamina (Figure 7L).
evidence: The Results section describes the desmosomal connectivity of MUSobP-neuV.

claim: The MUSac-neuPV cells can contract simultaneously with the parapodial retractor muscles (MUSobA-re), inducing parapodial retraction and a tilt of the aciculae with their proximal tip moving rostrally.
source: The MUSac-neuPV cells can contract simultaneously with the parapodial retractor muscles (MUSobA-re), inducing parapodial retraction and a tilt of the aciculae with their proximal tip moving rostrally (Figure 7J).
evidence: The Results section describes the coordinated contraction of two muscle types and the resulting movement.

claim: The retractor muscles form desmosomes on chaeFC-EC (epidermal chaetal follicle) and epidermal cells at their distal end in the neuropodium and anchor to ventral midline cells and the basal lamina at their other end.
source: The retractor muscles form desmosomes on chaeFC-EC (epidermal chaetal follicle) and epidermal cells at their distal end in the neuropodium and anchor to ventral midline cells and the basal lamina at their other end (Figure 7M).
evidence: The Results section describes the desmosomal connectivity of retractor muscles.

claim: During a startle response or crawling cycles, many muscles contract rapidly (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) and individual muscle contractions could not be spatially and temporally resolved.
source: We could only observe these spontaneous individual muscle contractions in non-crawling larvae. During a startle response or crawling cycles, many muscles contract rapidly (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) and we were not able to spatially and temporally resolve these to individual muscle groups.
evidence: The Results section describes the limitations of the imaging approach and cites a previous study.

claim: The availability of full desmosomal and synaptic connectomes (Verasztó et al., 2020) for the same Platynereis larva allowed analysis of how individual motoneurons could influence muscles and associated tissues.
source: The availability of full desmosomal and synaptic connectomes (Verasztó et al., 2020) for the same Platynereis larva allowed us to analyse how individual motoneurons could influence muscles and associated tissues.
evidence: The Results section describes the integration of synaptic and desmosomal data and cites the source of the synaptic connectome.

claim: By combining desmosomal and synaptic connectomes we can infer the impact of motoneuron activation on tissue movements.
source: Motoneuron activation is expected to induce postsynaptic muscle contraction, which will exert forces on the desmosomal partners of the muscle. By combining desmosomal and synaptic connectomes we can infer the impact of motoneuron activation on tissue movements (Figure 8).
evidence: The Results section describes the rationale for combining the two connectomes.

claim: 11 motoneuron types that are well developed in the 3-day-old larva were analyzed (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018; Verasztó et al., 2020).
source: We analysed 11 motoneuron types that are well developed in the 3-day-old larva (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018; Verasztó et al., 2020).
evidence: The Results section specifies the motoneuron types analyzed and cites previous studies.

claim: The 11 motoneuron types collectively provide broad innervation across the entire muscle network.
source: These collectively provide broad innervation across the entire muscle network (Figure 8A).
evidence: The Results section describes the overall pattern of motoneuron innervation.

claim: All motoneurons have multiple muscle targets and most muscles receive synapses from more than one motoneuron.
source: All motoneurons have multiple muscle targets and most muscles receive synapses from more than one motoneuron.
evidence: The Results section describes the convergence and divergence of motoneuron-muscle connections.

claim: When the most highly connected muscle in the parapodial complex (MUSchae-notAac) contracts, it is expected to transmit the forces of the contraction through desmosomes to up to nine distinct non-muscle cell types.
source: For example, when the most highly connected muscle in the parapodial complex (MUSchae-notAac) contracts, it is expected to transmit the forces of the contraction through desmosomes to up to nine distinct non-muscle cell types (Figure 9).
evidence: The Results section provides an example of the extent of tissue influenced by a single muscle contraction.

claim: There are eight motoneuron cell types that innervate the parapodial complex (MNcrab, MNbiramous, MNwave, MNspider-ant, MNspider-post, MNhose, MNchae, and MNring).
source: There are eight motoneuron cell types that innervate the parapodial complex (MNcrab, MNbiramous, MNwave, MNspider-ant, MNspider-post, MNhose, MNchae, and MNring).
evidence: The Results section lists the motoneuron types that innervate the parapodial complex.

claim: Each of the eight motoneuron types innervating the parapodial complex innervates a unique combination of muscle targets – not a single muscle type.
source: Each of these innervates a unique combination of muscle targets – not a single muscle type (Figure 10).
evidence: The Results section describes the specificity of motoneuron innervation patterns.

claim: The unique innervation patterns suggest the concerted activity of anatomically distinct muscle types during the parapodial crawl cycle and other appendage movements.
source: This suggests the concerted activity of anatomically distinct muscle types during the parapodial crawl cycle and other appendage movements.
evidence: The Results section infers functional coordination from innervation patterns.

claim: The reconstructions revealed the high diversity of muscle cell types in the larva.
source: Here, we reconstructed the somatic musculature and attached tissues in the nereid larva and showed how adhesion networks can be analysed for an entire body. We call this approach desmosomal connectomics, where the desmosomal connectome comprises all cells and extracellular structures (basal lamina, aciculae, and chaeta) and their desmosomal connections. Our reconstructions revealed the high diversity of muscle cell types in the larva.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: The complexity of the nereid musculature contrasts to the relatively simple muscle architecture in the nematode C. elegans and the tadpole larva of the tunicate Ciona intestinalis.
source: The complexity of the nereid musculature contrasts to the relatively simple muscle architecture in the nematode C. elegans and the tadpole larva of the tunicate Ciona intestinalis.
evidence: The Discussion compares the complexity of the nereid musculature to other organisms.

claim: The C. elegans hermaphrodite has 95 body wall muscles all with a similar rhomboid shape (Gieseler et al., 2017).
source: The C. elegans hermaphrodite has 95 body wall muscles all with a similar rhomboid shape (Gieseler et al., 2017).
evidence: The Discussion cites a study on C. elegans muscle anatomy for comparison.

claim: In the C. intestinalis larva, there are 36 muscle cells of 10 types (Nakamura et al., 2012).
source: In the C. intestinalis larva, there are 36 muscle cells of 10 types (Nakamura et al., 2012).
evidence: The Discussion cites a study on Ciona muscle anatomy for comparison.

claim: In contrast, the 3-day-old nereid larva has 853 muscle cells belonging to 53 types.
source: In contrast, the 3-day-old nereid larva has 853 muscle cells belonging to 53 types.
evidence: The Discussion contrasts the nereid larva with C. elegans and Ciona.

claim: A large number of muscles engage in the movement of the parapodial muscle complex.
source: A large number of muscles engage in the movement of the parapodial muscle complex.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes a key finding about the parapodial complex.

claim: The diversity of nereid somatic muscles is due to the presence of an endoskeleton.
source: This suggests that the diversity of nereid somatic muscles is due to the presence of an endoskeleton.
evidence: The Discussion proposes an explanation for muscle diversity.

claim: Polychaete annelids are the only animals outside the tetrapods that have trunk appendages rigidified by an endoskeleton.
source: Polychaete annelids are the only animals outside the tetrapods that have trunk appendages rigidified by an endoskeleton.
evidence: The Discussion states a unique anatomical feature of polychaetes.

claim: Aciculae probably evolved in the stem group of errant annelids around the Early Ordovician (Parry et al., 2019; Vinther et al., 2008) indicating the deep ancestry of these structures, predating tetrapod limbs.
source: Aciculae probably evolved in the stem group of errant annelids around the Early Ordovician (Parry et al., 2019; Vinther et al., 2008) indicating the deep ancestry of these structures, predating tetrapod limbs.
evidence: The Discussion cites studies on the evolutionary origin of aciculae.

claim: In contrast to tetrapod limb bones, the aciculae are independent skeletal elements without joints.
source: In contrast to tetrapod limb bones, the aciculae are independent skeletal elements without joints.
evidence: The Discussion contrasts aciculae with tetrapod limb bones.

claim: The function of aciculae is similar to tetrapod limb bones in that they provide attachment sites for limb muscles and rigidity in the appendages during movement.
source: Their function is nevertheless similar in that they provide attachment sites for limb muscles and rigidity in the appendages during movement.
evidence: The Discussion compares the functional role of aciculae to tetrapod limb bones.

claim: In each parapodium, the two aciculae are moved by unique and shared sets of muscles and change their relative angle within a crawling cycle.
source: In each parapodium, the two aciculae are moved by unique and shared sets of muscles and change their relative angle within a crawling cycle.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes findings on acicular movements.

claim: The stereotypy of the desmosomal connections across segments and body sides suggests that the desmosomal connectome develops through a precisely specified connectivity code between cell types.
source: The stereotypy of the desmosomal connections across segments and body sides suggests that – analogous to the synaptic connectome – the desmosomal connectome develops through a precisely specified connectivity code between cell types.
evidence: The Discussion infers developmental mechanisms from the observed stereotypy.

claim: Some desmosomal connections have a clear functional relevance, as the attachment of muscles to movable chitin structures.
source: Some of these connections have a clear functional relevance, as the attachment of muscles to movable chitin structures.
evidence: The Discussion interprets the functional significance of some desmosomal connections.

claim: Connections to locomotor ciliary cells may be due to proximity and the need for muscles to attach to something, alternatively, may mediate hitherto unexplored mechanistic interactions between muscular and ciliary locomotion or represent signalling connections (Green and Gaudry, 2000).
source: Others are more intriguing, such as the connections to locomotor ciliary cells. These may be due to proximity and the need for muscles to attach to something, alternatively, may mediate hitherto unexplored mechanistic interactions between muscular and ciliary locomotion or represent signalling connections (Green and Gaudry, 2000).
evidence: The Discussion speculates on the functional significance of connections to ciliary cells and cites a relevant study.

claim: The whole-body desmosomal connectome in combination with the synaptic connectome from the same volume (Verasztó et al., 2020) provide the foundation for understanding locomotor control in the nereid larva.
source: The whole-body desmosomal connectome described here in combination with the synaptic connectome from the same volume (Verasztó et al., 2020) provide the foundation for understanding locomotor control in the nereid larva.
evidence: The Discussion states the significance of the combined connectomes and cites the synaptic connectome study.

claim: In a crawling larva, the contraction of a large number of muscles is recruited in a precise temporal order in each limb to execute a full appendage cycle.
source: In a crawling larva, the contraction of a large number of muscles is recruited in a precise temporal order in each limb to execute a full appendage cycle.
evidence: The Discussion describes the coordination of muscle contractions during crawling.

claim: The limb movements are organised into a gait sequence, starting from the posterior-most segment.
source: The limb movements are organised into a gait sequence, starting from the posterior-most segment (Figure 7).
evidence: The Discussion describes the spatial organization of the gait sequence.

claim: The imaging of spontaneous muscle twitches, prediction of unit acicular movements and analysis of motoneuron innervation are the first steps towards understanding parapodial movements and their neuronal control.
source: Our imaging of spontaneous muscle twitches (Figure 8), prediction of unit acicular movements (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and analysis of motoneuron innervation (Figure 9) are the first steps towards understanding parapodial movements and their neuronal control.
evidence: The Discussion summarizes the contributions of the study towards understanding locomotor control.

claim: The availability of a laboratory culture, whole-body connectome and a growing repertoire of genetic tools make the nereid larva a promising experimental system for the in-depth analysis of locomotor control.
source: The availability of a laboratory culture, whole-body connectome and a growing repertoire of genetic tools make the nereid larva a promising experimental system for the in-depth analysis of locomotor control.
evidence: The Discussion argues for the utility of the nereid larva as a model system.

claim: In Platynereis, as well as in other animals, understanding and accurately modelling locomotion will require analysing nervous activity and synaptic contacts, as well as comprehensive maps of the adhesive networks of muscle systems.
source: We argue that in Platynereis, as well as in other animals, understanding and accurately modelling locomotion will not only require analysing nervous activity and synaptic contacts, but also comprehensive maps of the adhesive networks of muscle systems.
evidence: The Discussion argues for the importance of studying both synaptic and desmosomal networks.
